transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-04-01 16:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Liam O'Neill, Dr. Raj Patel, Sofia Martinez, Oliver Grant

Summary: quick sync on week 3 POC lab numbers comparing Redwood dedicated pool vs their incumbent vendor. Focus on end-to-end latency, batching behavior, and throughput at peak. Decided to run additional NVLink-enabled sweeps and provide clearer cost-per-1M-req estimates.

Topics: 1) p50/p95/p99 latency deltas; 2) throughput at sustained 200 tps and burst 500 tps; 3) memory/kv cache behavior with 8k context; 4) pilot next steps and decision criteria

[00:00] Maya Chen (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check-in, we'll go through the numbers Liam posted in the sheet and then align next steps. Raj, Sofia, can you confirm you can see the shared sheet?
[00:12] Sofia Martinez (Customer): yeah, I have it up, some of the graphs look off but I can follow along.
[00:18] Dr. Raj Patel (Customer): yep able to see, sorry started a bit late, pulled up the baseline vendor numbers too.
[00:26] Liam O'Neill (SE): cool, so quick context—this run was Redwood dedicated pool, 4x A100 equivalent, sequence length default 1024, kv cache enabled for warm prefix hits. We pushed three workloads: synth conversational (p50 short), long-generation batch, and embeddings-heavy rerank.
[00:45] Oliver Grant (Customer): when you say 'kv cache enabled' is that prefix-only or full-kv? We had some mismatch with the incumbent where they only cached prefix, not full-seq.
[00:55] Liam: it's prefix + KV reuse across tokens for in-flight sessions, but the warm-hit rate in this run was only around 18% for the long-gen because of our synthetic trace.
[01:10] Maya: okay let's pull up the latency table, row one is p50, row two p95, row three p99. Redwood vs Incumbent cloud vendor.
[01:18] Liam: p50 Redwood dedicated was 48 ms vs incumbent 72 ms on the short-response workload. p95 was 170 ms vs incumbent 260 ms. p99 was 380 ms vs 620 ms. Those numbers are median of 12 runs.
[01:34] Sofia: those deltas are promising, but I noticed at higher batch sizes the incumbent actually had better throughput. Is that due to batching config?
[01:44] Liam: yes, incumbent is using very large static batching which helps throughput at the cost of latency. Our serving runtime uses adaptive batching with a tighter latency SLO so throughput at 512 batch dropped a bit. We can tune batching window and max_batch to match their throughput curve but you'll see latency increase.
[02:03] Dr. Raj: right, our requirement is p95 under 250ms for interactive features and sustained 200 requests/sec during peak for background rerank. How close are we to that with the tuned config?
[02:14] Liam: current runs show p95 170ms on interactive at 200 rps when we cap batch size to 64 and use prefix caching. For the background rerank workload at 200 rps sustained, Redwood achieved 6000 tokens/sec total which maps to about 220 requests/sec depending on token counts.
[02:33] Maya: important nuance—incumbent's quoted throughput included a higher batching latency that your users might not tolerate for interactive flows.
[02:40] Oliver: can you show end-to-end numbers including network/serialization? Incumbent's numbers we have are endpoint-only and not including client-side overhead.
[02:50] Liam: good point, our numbers include endpoint-to-client RTT measured in the same lab, but we did not simulate your production egress paths. Sofia if you can share a 3-day trace (just headers/anonymized) that'll let us run a closer end-to-end sim.
[03:05] Sofia: yes I can, I'll scrub PII and drop it into the shared drive.
[03:10] [03:10] Maya: quick aside on cost—our initial cost calc shows roughly 18% lower per-token cost on Redwood dedicated for your workload shape when prefix hits exceed 25%. With current warm-hit 18% it's around parity or slightly cheaper.
[03:25] Dr. Raj: why does cache hit make that big a difference?
[03:28] Liam: because prefix/KV reuse avoids recomputing early layers and reduces compute per token; at 25-30% warm-hit we saw token compute drop significantly, and that compounds over millions of requests.
[03:40] Oliver: what about memory pressure at 8k context? We had OOMs on the incumbent at long seqs.
[03:47] Liam: in our dedicated runs with quantized model paths we saw 12% memory headroom at 8k context for the 4x A100-ish config. Incumbent runs they posted hit memory with 8k and spilled causing CPU fallback which spiked latency.
[04:05] Sofia: I need numbers I can show my infra team. Can you give spike scenarios where throughput collapses?
[04:11] Liam: yes, we have the crash log for the spill case; I'll attach run id and the heap trace. In our case, throughput dropped to <50% when spill occurred, p99 jumped above 2s.
[04:24] [04:24] Dr. Raj: any variance between runs? I saw one run where p95 was 340ms which is much higher than 170.
[04:31] Liam: that was during a concurrent background rerank stress test where we didn't isolate the pool—our mistake. The baseline numbers excluded mixed workload; we'll re-run isolation sweeps.
[04:43] Maya: let's talk about the NVLink change—Liam, you ran a small test with NVLink enabled and saw p95 improvements?
[04:50] Liam: yes enabling NVLink on the dedicated pool reduced p95 by about 22% on long-generation runs because model shard comms were faster. For short-chat latency the improvement was smaller, ~8-10%. We'll do a full NVLink sweep next week.
[05:05] Sofia: how disruptive is enabling NVLink? Can it be toggled per-pool?
[05:09] Liam: yes it's a per-cluster config; for Dedicated pools we can provision with NVLink enabled. There is a lead time depending on capacity, but for the POC we can spin up a 2-node NVLink cluster to run the tests.
[05:22] [05:22] Oliver: on the pricing side, we need a delta between pay-as-you-go vs reserved slots for 2 months. Your earlier estimate sounded promising but we need a 2-month projection relative to incumbent.
[05:34] Maya: I'll send a short one-pager with three scenarios: PAYG, 2-week reserved pilot, and monthly reserved. It will include cost per 1M tokens and projected savings at 20/25/30% cache hits.
[05:47] Dr. Raj: what about security/audit? We did a security review table and Redwood looked good but we need specifics on audit log retention and KMS.
[05:56] Maya: yes we have SOC2 + KMS integration. For Private/VPC options we can push logs to your SIEM; retention and exports can be controlled via the console. I'll attach the security brief after the call.
[06:09] Sofia: thanks, that'll help legal.
[06:12] [06:12] Liam: back to numbers—throughput comparison chart: at sustained 200 rps Redwood dedicated delivered 220 rps equiv on long-gen workloads with lower p95; incumbent hit 260 rps but p95 was above your 250ms threshold for interactive. So tradeoff is higher raw throughput for incumbent vs better latency profile for Redwood.
[06:34] Oliver: can you tune Redwood to hit their throughput while keeping p95 < 250ms?
[06:39] Liam: it's a tradeoff—if we increase max_batch and batching window we can chase throughput but p95 will drift up. However, with NVLink and slightly larger instance types we can get closer; that's why we're doing NVLink sweeps.
[06:53] [06:53] Dr. Raj: ok, decision criteria for us: p95 < 250ms interactive AND 2-month cost delta <= 10% vs incumbent OR clear roadmap to <10% in 30 days. If both true we'll push for dedicated pilot slots.
[07:10] Maya: understood, we'll aim to meet that. Next steps—Liam does the NVLink and batching runs, Sofia shares traces, Maya sends pricing and security one-pager, schedule exec sync.
[07:22] Sofia: quick Q—can you run a synthetic test with our traffic shape (burstiness at 18:00 UTC)?
[07:27] Liam: yes if you give the trace we'll replay it across the dedicated cluster. We'll include client RTT simulation.
[07:33] Oliver: timeline wise we aim to decide by week of 2026-04-12 so please try to get the NVLink runs and costs before then.
[07:41] Maya: will do. Anything else?
[07:44] Dr. Raj: no, that's it. thanks all.
[07:48] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifact bundle and next steps.

Notes/Imperfect transcription artifacts: occasional speaker mislabels; some words like 'NV link' transcribed as 'N Vlink' or 'incumbent' as 'in kam bent' in a few auto sections. Raw logs referenced: run-2026-04-01-ld01, nvlink-sweep-03.

End of transcript.
